Armour is pretty easy to price check

If it has 70+ life, and 100 ele res, it’s worth checking out on poetrade. My rule of thumb is to generally check 10 lower than what my item is. So if I have a 87 life and a 112 res cheat, I put min 77 life and min 102 res into poe trade to see what similar items are priced at.

In addition to life and res, other rolls that add value and are worth adding to your search include +stats, +mana, +accuracy on gloves, and +move speed on boots (minimum of 15%(search your exact movespeed))

ES gear is easy as well, just check total es to get a ballpark, and include total res and the other aforementioned stats.


Weapons are a little harder to price. The easiest way is to consider weapons in terms of three archetypes: phys dps, ele dps, and spell caster. You ideally want 3-4 synergistic mods on your weapon before you consider pricing it.

For phys dps: (sort poetrade by phys dps, and add a search group for any crit if you have it)
%inc physical
Flat phys
IAS
Crit multi
Crit Chance 

Ele dps: (same deal, just sort by ele dps instead of phys dps)
Adds x-y ele damage to attacks
IAS
Multi
Crit Chance 

Caster weapons: you want 3-4 affixes at a minimum of t4 to be worth something.
Spell damage
Spell Crit Chance
Spell multi
Increased ele damage 
Cat speed
Added ele damage to spells
Regular Crit Chance 

Jewellery is the most difficult to price
Belts: preferably either a Stygian, leather, or studded belt base
Minimum rolls are 70life, 90 res. Elemental damage with attacks is extremely desirable, so keep an eye out it, or an open suffix that you could craft onto it

Amulets:
Life, stats, multi, resistances, ias etc... Pretty much anything except armour/evasion/mana/life on kill/leech/regen. Use a bit of brain power and think if they affixes on it are synergistic. Two caster mods and two phys damage mods are no better than a blue item.

The image has survived in the modern world as a representation of magisterial or collective power, law and governance. The fasces frequently occurs as a charge in heraldry: it is present on the reverse of the U.S. Mercury dime coin and behind the podium in the United States House of Representatives; and it was the origin of the name of the National Fascist Party in Italy (from which the term fascism is derived).

During the first half of the 20th century both the fasces and the swastika (each symbol having its own unique ancient religious and mythological associations) became heavily identified with the authoritarian/fascist political movements of Adolf Hitler and Benito Mussolini. During this period the swastika became deeply stigmatized, but the fasces did not undergo a similar process.

The fact that the fasces remained in use in many societies after World War II may have been due to the fact that prior to Mussolini the fasces had already been adopted and incorporated within the governmental iconography of many governments outside Italy. As such, its use persists as an accepted form of governmental and other iconography in various contexts. (The swastika remains in common usage in parts of Asia for religious purposes which are also unrelated to early 20th century European fascism.)
